laat_vaar.voor: Mense wat in 'n gebied gewoon het wat vir 'n ander groep verklaar is, moes wegtrek.
laat_vaar.na: Mense moes wegtrek as hulle in 'n gebied gewoon het wat vir 'n ander groep verklaar is.
laat_vaar.rede_vinder: Putting the main verb first removes the stacked 'wat ... wat' clauses before the verb and makes the sentence easier for a Grade 6 reader, with the same meaning.
laat_vaar.rede_keurder: The original reads clearly and ends on 'moes wegtrek', which the next sentence's 'Ons noem dit' points back to; moving the verb forward leaves 'dit' after 'verklaar is' and loosens that link, so the change is lateral at best and disturbs a neighbour.

vlae.teks: Die regering bou ook huise en bring water, elektrisiteit en paaie daarheen.
vlae.rede: 'daarheen' has no clear place to point to (the previous sentence names no place), and 'bring ... paaie' is an odd collocation; the list is protected, so the writer should say where the services go without guessing here.

beskerm_bedenkings.rede: In 'Kimberley en Johannesburg is 'n duidelike voorbeeld daarvan' two subjects take a singular 'voorbeeld'; it reads acceptably as one joint example, but 'duidelike voorbeelde' would agree in number. Left unchanged because it is protected.

laat_vaar_vorige.voor: die vangs afgelaai en verwerk word
laat_vaar_vorige.na: die vangs afgelaai en verwerk kan word
laat_vaar_vorige.rede_vinder: The modal 'kan' of the first part should carry into the parallel passive clause.
laat_vaar_vorige.rede_keurder: The original passive clause is grammatical, and adding 'kan' changes a statement into a possibility for no clear gain.

laat_vaar_vorige.rede_vinder: 'ontstaan' is the standard word for a town coming into being and matches the rest of the lesson.
laat_vaar_vorige.rede_keurder: 'opgekom' is natural Afrikaans for towns springing up, so 'ontstaan' is a lateral swap.

laat_vaar_vorige.rede_vinder: 'dra ... vorm' is an unnatural calque; towns 'het' a shape.
laat_vaar_vorige.rede_keurder: 'dra nog daardie vorm' is acceptable Afrikaans and carries the sense of bearing a past imprint, which plain 'het' loses.
